items.why: The report says "Both spectra show graphene G (about 1580 cm-1) and 2D (2681 cm-1 on Au, 2696 cm-1 on Cu), so graphene is present on both metals."

It gives D at 1344.2 cm-1 on Au with "I(D)/I(G) (heights) = 0.97 ± 0.09", and on Cu "I(D)/I(G) = 0.6 ± 0.2" with D "only a weak, low-confidence feature", which matches the rubric numbers and the poor constraint.

It says only in general terms that "Strain frozen in by fast cooling is a plausible contributor" and that "liquid-to-solid change on solidification adds strain"; it never ties this to the stronger D band on Au or presents it as the authors' hypothesis.

It reads the strong D as a sign of defects ("likely higher defect density on Au") and tests strain against the G and 2D shifts using the Lee 2012 slope, but it never states that D needs defects or edges to be activated, or that strain alone cannot produce D.

It asks "What was the laser wavelength?" and explains that "I(D)/I(G) scales with lambda^4" and that D and 2D "disperse with excitation energy (about 52 and 100 cm-1/eV)", so L_D and the positions cannot be compared without it.
It warns that "The Cu spectrum is low signal-to-noise... G, D and their ratios on Cu have errors of 20-35 %, and the G width is essentially unconstrained", and quotes errors throughout.

wrong_claims.why: It explicitly declines: "L_D_nm: Not computed. The relation needs the laser wavelength, which is not recorded."
It never says strain causes the Au D peak; it says "No mechanism is proven by these data" and calls strain only "a plausible contributor".
